# My plan for this year

Well, I've been doing wheat and maize on these 20 mu for a long time now, same as almost everyone in the village. My father did it this way too. I don't change much unless I see a good reason. This year looks like a normal year so far, so I'll mostly do what I did last year — that gave me a decent harvest, around 450 kg of wheat per mu and a bit more maize.

**Wheat** goes in the ground around mid-October, right after I clear the maize stalks. I buy improved seed from the agricultural shop in the county — I used to save my own but the neighbor Lao Wang got much better wheat when he bought fresh seed, so most of us do that now. Before planting I spread about one bag of compound fertilizer (the 15-15-15 kind) per mu, maybe a little less, then the tractor guy comes to till and plant in one pass. I pay him by the mu. In spring when the wheat greens up and starts jointing, I topdress another bag of urea per mu — that's the most important one, my father always said "wheat lives on the spring fertilizer." I irrigate with my share of the village well, usually four times: once before winter to hold the soil, then at green-up, at jointing, and again when the grain is filling. The water costs add up because we pay by the meter now. I'll spray herbicide once in spring, and if I see aphids I'll mix in some insecticide. Harvest in early June with a hired combine.

**Maize** goes straight into the wheat stubble within a few days of harvest — no time to till properly, that's how everyone does it now with the no-till planter. I use hybrid seed, whatever the shop recommends, something that finishes before the frost. One bag of compound goes in with the seed, then urea at the big trumpet stage before tasseling. Maize usually gets enough rain in July and August so I only irrigate once or twice if it's dry. Harvest late September so I can get the wheat back in on time.

My wife and I do most of the work. My two older children help on weekends when they're home from school, but I hire help for harvest and some of the spraying because the window is short. I keep a bit of cash back in case something goes wrong — a bad spray, a broken pump, my mother getting sick. I'd rather have the money than squeeze another bag of fertilizer in.
